newsitem.title: JAPAN: Mazda not seen aided by minicar decision.
newsitem.headline: Mazda not seen aided by minicar decision.

text.p: Mazda Motor Corp's decision to scrap its minicar operation will have little impact on the troubled carmaker's earnings, analysts said, adding that the company still needs to restructure its manufacturing plants.
Mazda, 33.4 percent owned by Ford Motor Co, is expected to pull out of production and development of mini passenger cars to save costs, industry sources said.
"It's a good decision as it will reduce fixed costs, but it will have little impact (on Mazda's earnings)," said Nikko Research senior analyst Noriyuki Matsushima.

Ford's Henry Wallace, who slipped into the driving seat of Mazda as the first foreigner to head a major Japanese company last June, has been trying to steer Mazda to stay out of the red in its earnings.
Mazda has been posting operating losses since 1993/94 business year as its new models in its mainstay compact and luxury sedans failed to lure Japanese customers.

Dropping the minicar development is a step toward reducing fixed costs, but Mazda needs to raise its efficiency at its Hofu plant, in Yamaguchi prefecture in western Japan, producing medium-priced and luxury cars, Matsushima said.

Mazda should take cost control a step further by integrating plants or disposing of idle lines, like the Ujina Number three line in Hiroshima which was shut down in 1993 due to poor minicar sales, analysts said.
Production at Hofu plant is at 50 percent of its output capacity, but the Ujina plant runs at full capacity now, helped by good demand for recreation vehicles such as the Demio model.

There will be no production of new models at Hofu until the company's new Capella model is launched this summer, and even that would not be enough to drastically raise the plant's production efficiency, analysts said.
Hofu has output capacity for 400,000 vehicles a year.
Mazda officials would not comment on the possible pullout of minicar development or its reasons.
"We cannot comment about our future new models. We will continue selling mini vehicles," a Mazda spokesman said.
Mazda has been selling the Suzuki-made 660cc commercial vehicles since June 1989 and the 660cc Carol car, using a Suzuki-made engine and chassis since November 1989.
Sales of the Carol, which has a Mazda-developed body, fell by about 10,000 in 1996 from the previous year to 17,635 cars.
Mazda sold 334,382 vehicles including mini vehicles in Japan last year, the sixth straight year of decline, after a peak of 600,000 vehicles in 1990.
Japan's Transport Ministry is set to change its classifications of mini vehicles effective October 1998 in order to enhance collision safety and allowing makers to produce longer and wider bodies.
Carmakers do not disclose actual car development costs but the development of a car will cost several billion yen (several tens of million dollars).

In November, Mazda had forecast a zero parent operating profit and a parent current profit of 11 billion yen ($95.6 million) in the year to March 1997 compared to an operating loss of 12.64 billion yen ($109 million) and current profit of 1.20 billion yen ($10.4 million) the year before.

Matsushima sees the company posting an operating loss of three billion yen ($26.0 million) in 1996/97 and current profit of 10 billion yen ($86.9 million), in line with Mazda's own forecast of 11 billion yen ($95.6 million), helped by a weaker yen against the dollar and income from selling stock holdings.
"Mazda is likely to start another step in restructuring its manufacturing structure. It should do it because the Japanese car market has become tougher," Matsushima said.
